Abstract
Situated within the Neurocash ® framework for measuring implicit emotional and cognitive responses, this 
review examines the human voice as a non-invasive psychophysiological marker. It outlines the physiological 
mechanisms of voice production and explains how emotional states influence breathing, vocal-fold vibration 
and articulation, shaping acoustic features such as pitch and intensity. The review then examines Speech 
Emotion Recognition as the main approach for extracting emotional information from speech, describing 
the methodological pipeline from emotional speech databases and preprocessing to classification using 
traditional machine-learning algorithms and modern deep-learning and self-supervised models. The analysis 
concludes that no single computational approach is universally optimal, as performance depends on 
language, emotional categories, data quality and environmental conditions. Overall, this review provides an 
interdisciplinary framework linking psychophysiology, vocal acoustics and artificial intelligence to support 
Neurocash® studies on cognitive workload, perceived security and implicit trust in cash design.
Keywords: acoustic feature extraction, affective computing, implicit emotion perception, multimodal 
emotion analysis, psychophysiology, self-supervised representation learning, Speech Emotion Recognition, 
Neurocash®, cash design.
JEL classification:  C55, C80, D91.

Resumen
A partir de la metodología Neurocash ® para el estudio de las respuestas emocionales y cognitivas 
implícitas, en este documento se examina la voz humana como un marcador psicofisiológico no invasivo. 
En primer lugar, se describen los mecanismos fisiológicos de producción de la voz y se explica cómo los 
estados emocionales modifican la respiración, la vibración de las cuerdas vocales y la articulación, lo 
que altera características acústicas como el tono y la intensidad. A continuación, se analiza el sistema de 
reconocimiento de emociones en el habla (SER, por sus siglas en inglés) como la principal herramienta para 
extraer información emocional a partir de la voz, describiendo su proceso metodológico desde la selección 
de bases de datos y el preprocesamiento hasta la clasificación mediante algoritmos de aprendizaje 
automático clásico y modelos de aprendizaje profundo y autosupervisado. El análisis concluye que no 
existe un modelo universalmente óptimo y proporciona un marco interdisciplinar para apoyar estudios 
Neurocash® sobre carga cognitiva, seguridad percibida y confianza implícita en el diseño del efectivo.

1 Introduction
Cash design is not only a matter of visual aesthetics and security features, but also of how people implicitly 
perceive, interpret, and emotionally respond to cash during daily interactions. In this context, voice analysis offers 
a promising bridge between cash perception research and psychophysiological measurement, as vocal signals 
can reflect subtle changes in emotional arousal, cognitive load, confidence, and perceived security. Understanding 
these implicit human reactions is fundamental in cash design to optimize currency usability and the effectiveness 
of anti-counterfeiting measures.
The aim of this review is to offer a broad and connected perspective on voice analysis, encompassing 
the physiological bases of vocal production, its relationship with emotional expression, and the technological 
tools currently available for extracting acoustic features in perception and affective-computing research. In doing 
so, the work synthesizes the present state of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) technologies while preserving 
a conceptual and accessible perspective grounded in psychology. Rather than offering an exhaustive technical 
review of every computational component, the goal is to present a coherent, interdisciplinary overview that bridges 
psychophysiology, acoustics, and machine-learning approaches to emotional voice analysis.
SER is situated within the broader domain of Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER), a field that integrates multiple 
biosignals, such as EEG (electroencephalography), facial expressions, gestures, or speech, to infer affective states. Within 
this ecosystem, the human voice stands out as a unique psychophysiological signal: it arises from the coordination of 
breathing, vocal-fold movement, and articulation, all of which change with emotional, cognitive, and autonomic states (De 
Lope & Graña, 2023). Understanding these biological mechanisms is therefore essential for interpreting how emotions 
shape the acoustic signal. For this reason, the document begins by outlining the physiological and anatomical bases of 
vocal production, following authors who argue that acoustic analyses must be grounded in vocal biomechanics.
Building on this theoretical foundation, the second section examines how emotional states influence key acoustic 
features such as fundamental frequency, intensity, spectral balance, and temporal dynamics. Recent reviews show 
that emotions reliably shape vocal acoustics, allowing speech to convey meaningful psychophysiological information 
(Van Puyvelde et al., 2018; Schewski et al., 2025). These relationships are central both to psychological research and 
to the development of computational models that aim to decode emotions from speech.
The study then presents the complete Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) methodological pipeline, 
outlining the process of transforming raw audio into emotional labels. These stages include audio-source selection, 
preprocessing, acoustic feature extraction, and classification using either classical machine-learning algorithms or 
modern deep-learning architectures. 
Finally, after describing the pipeline, the document provides a structured overview of the most relevant 
technological tools for implementing SER, ranging from commercial to open-source options. This includes 
commercial approaches (e.g., audEERING, iMotions), pretrained model pipelines with external or internal classifiers, 
custom SER systems built from scratch, and modular multimodal frameworks such as the MixedEmotions Toolbox.
By comparing these alternatives, practical considerations that researchers must evaluate when selecting 
tools for academic or applied contexts are highlighted, including model interpretability, data requirements, and 
computational costs.

Although this review focuses on the human voice as a neurophysiological marker for implicit emotion, 
it is motivated by the broader research context of neurodesign for cash. Within the Neurocash ® framework, 
the Innovation & Development unit of the Banco de España aims to establish an objective, multidimensional 
methodology to evaluate the public’s perception of banknotes. By integrating neuroscientific tools and implicit 
behavioral measures, this project seeks to overcome the traditional limitations of subjective surveys, capturing the 
subconscious emotional and cognitive reactions of users when interacting with currency (Banco de España, n.d.; 
Ortuño et al., 2020). 
Specifically applied to cash perception research, the Neurocash ® methodology provides cash designers 
with a robust, quantitative tool to optimize the design process. By capturing these acoustic fluctuations during 
exposure to or evaluation of currency features, the human voice can complement other biometric and behavioral 
measures within this framework. This allows for the precise evaluation of how different visual and tactile elements 
capture attention, how cognitive workload is modulated during the verification of security features, and how these 
factors influence the user’s implicit trust and perceived security (Banco de España, n.d.; Ortuño et al., 2020). By 
systematically analyzing these biometric, neurophysiological, and vocal responses, Neurocash ® acts as a scientific 
bridge that enhances the aesthetics, intuitive usability, and anti-counterfeiting resilience of banknotes throughout 
their entire lifecycle.
1.1 Justification of the review
Despite the rapid growth of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), existing reviews remain fragmented and often focus 
on only one part of the field. Most surveys highlight technical advances, especially, new machine-learning models 
and self-supervised speech methods, while giving much less attention to the psychophysiological and acoustic 
principles that support emotional expression in the voice. As a result, many overviews adopt a mainly computational 
viewpoint, with limited connection to the biological mechanisms of vocal production or to the well-established 
acoustic markers of emotion.
This limitation in the review literature reflects a broader problem in the field: a lack of integration across 
disciplines. Psychophysiology, vocal acoustics, and deep-learning-based SER systems are often treated as separate 
research areas, even though they naturally depend on one another. Because of this separation, key concepts, such 
as subglottal pressure changes, vocal-fold behaviour, prosodic shifts, and spectral patterns, rarely appear together 
in computational surveys. This reduces the interpretability of SER models and makes it harder to understand the 
psychophysiological meaning of the features these systems extract.
A further challenge is that research on how emotions influence vocal acoustics is spread across different 
fields such as clinical voice science, neuroscience, phonetics, and machine learning. Because these findings are 
rarely brought together, it is difficult to build a clear, unified understanding of how emotional processes shape the 
voice and how these cues are used in SER systems.
For these reasons, an integrative review that unifies physiological mechanisms, acoustic correlates, 
psychological theory, and contemporary SER methodologies is necessary. The present work aims to consolidate 
these domains into a coherent conceptual framework, offering the scientific community a comprehensive, 
interdisciplinary account of how emotions are encoded and decoded through the human voice.

2 Methods
This article was written as a narrative integrative review, a method that brings together different types of evidence 
from fields such as psychophysiology, acoustics, speech science, affective computing, and machine learning. This 
type of review makes it possible to combine empirical studies, theoretical work, technical documentation, and 
methodological papers to create a broad understanding of a research area. Because Speech Emotion Recognition 
(SER) involves many disciplines, this approach is well suited to summarizing its physiological, acoustic, and 
computational aspects within a single framework.
2.1 Search Strategy and Sources
Between October 2025 and February 2026, a broad literature search was performed across the following databases 
and platforms:
• Google Scholar
• PubMed (physiology, voice science)
• IEEE Xplore (machine learning, signal processing)
• ACM Digital Library [Human Computer Interaction (HCI), affective computing]
• arXiv (deep learning and transformer-based SER studies)
• Publisher websites for technical documentation (e.g., audEERING, iMotions, Affectiva, Microsoft, and 
Amazon Web Services)
• GitHub repositories for open-source SER toolkits.
The search combined keywords and Boolean operators such as:
“speech emotion recognition” OR “SER” OR “emotional prosody” OR “acoustic correlates of emotion” OR 
“self-supervised speech models” OR “wav2vec2” OR “HuBERT” OR “WavLM” OR “affective computing” OR “voice 
physiology” OR “emotion acoustics”.
2.2 Inclusion Criteria
Sources were included if they met at least one of the following criteria:
• Conceptual relevance to the physiological, psychological, or computational foundations of emotional voice 
production (e.g., Liebenthal et al., 2016).
• Empirical or methodological contribution to acoustic correlates of emotion, vocal stress, or prosody (e.g., 
Van Puyvelde et al., 2018; Schewski et al., 2025).

3 Definition and Applications of SER
3.1 Definition
Within the broader field of Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER), which includes analyses based on EEG, gestures, 
facial expressions, and other biometric signals, we find Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), whose primary 
function is to convert audio into text. This process relies on signal processing and machine learning methods that 
are shared with emotion related systems (De Lope & Graña, 2023).
One of ASR’s key subfields is Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), which uses similar signal processing 
tools such as speech rate, pitch, and prosody to identify and classify emotions present in speech. Recent work 
highlights the importance of these acoustic cues in predicting emotional states accurately (Van Puyvelde et al., 
2018; Schewski et al., 2025).
3.2 Applications 
SER is used in many areas, including psychology, healthcare, and marketing. However, for the purposes of this 
work, in the context of implicit perception measurement, we focus on its role within the Internet of Things (IoT). 
In IoT environments, devices interact continuously with users, and emotional information can help these systems 
adjust their behaviour, personalise their responses, and create more natural interactions (Chang et al., 2024). The 
IoT ecosystem includes several interaction focused fields, such as Human–Computer Interaction (HCI), Human–
Machine Interaction (HMI), Human–Robot Interaction (HRI), and Affective Computing.
Within this ecosystem, SER becomes especially relevant for Affective Computing, a field whose goal 
is to detect and interpret human emotions so that systems can adapt affectively. This “affective layer” is what 
distinguishes Affective Computing from other interaction oriented disciplines:
• HCI, HMI, and HRI focus on the mechanics and design of interaction, such as interfaces, usability, 
ergonomics, and task performance, without necessarily analysing emotional states.
• Affective Computing, in contrast, explicitly incorporates emotion. It studies how machines can understand 
and respond to the user’s affective signals (Wang et al., 2022), making SER a key component for enabling 
emotionally adaptive behaviour.

4 Voice Physiology and Acoustic Correlates of Emotion
As illustrated in Figure 1, voice production begins with airflow originating in the lungs. The vocal folds, two bands of 
tissue located in the larynx between the base of the tongue and the top of the trachea, remain open during breathing 
and close during phonation (National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders [NIDCD, n.d.]). When 
speaking, the diaphragm contracts to expand the thoracic cavity, allowing the lungs to fill with air before releasing 
it during exhalation, which initiates the phonatory process (Ladefoged, 2001). Sound is produced when exhaled 
air passes through the closed vocal folds, increasing subglottal pressure until they separate, allowing air to flow 
through the glottis. The glottis widens during breathing and narrows during voice production (NIDCD, n.d.; Zhang, 
2016). Rapid airflow creates pressure changes that bring the vocal folds back together, causing them to vibrate 
and generate sound. Typical speech requires normal vibratory behaviour of both the larynx and the vocal folds 
(Morrison, Rammage, Nichol, Pullan, & May, 1994).
Once phonation is understood, further components of speech production can be defined, namely articulation 
and resonance. Vocal production relies on the coordinated action of several subsystems: 
• The respiratory phase: during which air exits the lungs (Morrison, Rammage, Nichol, Pullan, & May, 1994).

5 Emotions and their Influence on Acoustics
Emotions influence the way our voice sounds because they affect how we breathe, how the larynx is positioned, and 
how the vocal tract moves. In psychology, emotions are understood as complex reactions that include thoughts, bodily 
changes, and expressive behaviours, all of which can shape our vocal output (American Psychological Association 
[APA], n.d.). Research shows that emotional states modify key acoustic features, such as fundamental frequency (F0), 
loudness, spectral balance or voice quality, and timing, through physiological changes in subglottal pressure, vocal fold 
vibration, and the configuration of the vocal tract (Liebenthal et al., 2016; Van Puyvelde et al., 2018). For example, 
positive emotions often occur alongside facial and postural changes like smiling, which alter the shape of the vocal 
tract and tend to produce a higher, brighter ‑sounding voice. More generally, high ‑arousal emotions such as joy or 
anger are associated with louder voices and greater variation in intensity than low ‑arousal states like sadness 
or tenderness (Liebenthal et al., 2016).
Emotional and cognitive demands also influence vocal behaviour. When people are under cognitive–
emotional load, their voices show measurable shifts in F0, loudness, and perturbation ‑based voice measures, 
reflecting the combined effect of attention, mental effort, and affective state on vocal production (Van Mersbergen 
& Payne, 2021; Van Puyvelde et al., 2018). Clinical reviews further show that increased tension in the larynx can 
produce rougher voice quality and reduced vocal power, illustrating how physiological stress and emotional strain 
affect the sound of the voice (Eastwood et al., 2015). Taken together, these findings support the idea that emotions 
influence speech through coordinated changes in bodily, cognitive, and expressive systems, consistent with the 
three‑component model of emotion.
A growing body of research demonstrates that emotions also shape prosody, patterns of pitch, rhythm, 
and intonation, in reliable ways. A large review of speech produced under negative emotions, stress, and cognitive 
load shows that anger, fear, anxiety, and stress frequently involve increases in F0 and, in some cases, noticeable 
changes in speech rate or pausing, although results vary across studies (Schewski et al., 2025). Evidence from acted 
emotional speech in Mexican Spanish similarly reveals distinct prosodic profiles: emocionado [excited] and enojado 
[angry] show high F0 values, wide pitch movements, and rising bitonal accents, while tranquilo  [calm] and triste 
[sad] display flatter, more even pitch contours with smaller differences between syllables. Neutral utterances follow 
the expected declarative pattern typical of Central Mexican Spanish (González Franco et al., 2023).

6 Methodological Pipeline SER
Once we understand how the voice is produced and how emotions can shape it, we can look at how Speech Emotion 
Recognition (SER) systems go from a simple audio recording to identifying the emotion behind it. This process 
typically involves four stages:
• Audio source selection: Studies may employ spontaneous speech recordings or standardized emotional 
speech databases. Widely used corpora, such as EmoDB (Burkhardt et al., 2005), RAVDESS (Livingstone & 
Russo, 2018), and IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), provide controlled, annotated emotional material essential 
for SER benchmarking.
• Data preprocessing: Includes denoising, normalization, segmentation, and amplitude or sampling ‑rate 
standardization to ensure signal quality and consistency across recordings (De Lope & Graña, 2023).
• Feature extraction: Extracted acoustic features typically involve pitch, prosodic dynamics, spectral energy, 
speech rate, and voice quality. In many studies, researchers rely on standardized sets like eGeMAPS or 
openSMILE so that acoustic features remain comparable across different projects (Eyben et al., 2016).
• Classification approaches: SER tasks may be addressed using traditional machine ‑learning models (e.g., 
SVMs, Random Forests) as well as deep learning architectures (e.g., CNN ‑, RNN ‑, or transformer ‑based 
systems) trained on emotional speech databases (De Lope & Graña, 2023).

6.3 Feature extraction
A speech recording contains thousands of measurable acoustic properties, many of which are useful for Speech 
Emotion Recognition (SER). Recent reviews group these properties into several main categories, temporal, prosodic, 
spectral, cepstral, and energy‑related features, and describe standardized feature sets developed for paralinguistic 
analysis (De Lope & Graña, 2023; Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023).
6.3.1 Temporal and fluency features
Temporal features describe how speech unfolds over time. They include overall duration, speech rate, syllable timing, 
rhythm, and the presence or length of pauses, as well as distinctions between vocalic and non ‑vocalic segments. 
These patterns often change with emotional arousal or cognitive load and are frequently included in both traditional 
feature sets and deep‑learning SER models (Byun & Lee, 2021; De Lope & Graña, 2023).
6.3.2 Prosodic features
Prosodic features relate to pitch and loudness patterns, such as fundamental frequency (F0), intonation contours, 
intensity, accentuation, and overall variability. Because they reflect adjustments in phonation and respiration, 
prosodic cues are reliably associated with emotional expression in speech (Bhangale &  Kothandaraman, 2023; De 
Lope & Graña, 2023).
6.3.3 Spectral features
Spectral features capture how energy is distributed across frequencies. They include formants, spectral centroid, 
roll‑off, kurtosis, and various energy bands, as well as spectrogram‑based representations such as Mel‑spectrograms. 
These features reflect vocal ‑tract configuration and are essential in both classical machine ‑learning and deep 
learning–based SER systems (Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023).
6.3.4 Cepstral features
Widely used in speech and emotion recognition, cepstral coefficients such as MFCCs, delta and delta ‑delta 
coefficients, GFCCs, and LPCCs capture perceptually and physiologically meaningful aspects of the signal. Many 
SER studies adopt them as core inputs for both machine ‑learning and neural architectures (Byun & Lee, 2021; 
Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023). 
6.3.5 Energy‑based features
Energy features measure the overall power of the signal and its variation over time. Metrics such as root mean square 
(RMS) energy can help differentiate high ‑arousal from low‑arousal emotional states (Bhangale &  Kothandaraman, 
2023).

6.4 Classifier Approaches: Conventional (Classical Machine Learning) vs. Deep Learning
Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems are commonly divided into two major methodological families. The 
first relies on conventional machine ‑learning models built on hand ‑crafted acoustic features, while the second 
uses deep learning techniques that learn informative representations directly from the speech signal or from its 
time–frequency transformations. This section provides an overview of the modelling assumptions, typical input 
features, representative algorithms, and the main advantages and limitations associated with each approach. A 
comprehensive survey of the field discusses these developments in detail and motivates the comparison presented 
here (Kaur & Singh, 2023).
6.4.1 Conventional methods (classical machine learning)
• Modelling pipeline: Conventional Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) methods begin by extracting a set 
of hand-crafted features from the audio signal. These features describe core aspects of the voice, such 
as pitch, loudness, rhythmic patterns, and widely used acoustic descriptors like Mel-Frequency Cepstral 
Coefficients (MFCCs), which summarise how energy is distributed across frequency bands. After these 
features are obtained, they are passed to a traditional machine-learning classifier, such as Support Vector 
Machines, k-Nearest Neighbours, Naïve Bayes, decision trees or Random Forests, Gaussian Mixture Models, 
or Hidden Markov Models, which learns to distinguish between emotional categories. Because these 
features are manually designed rather than learned automatically, this approach tends to work reliably 
even when only limited training data are available. It is also generally considered more transparent and 
easier to interpret than modern deep-learning systems. MFCCs, in particular, have a long history in speech 
processing research, originating in the influential work of Davis and Mermelstein (1980).
• Representative classifiers:
 — Support Vector Machines (SVMs): SVMs try to find the best boundary that separates different emotion 
classes in the feature space, keeping the classes as far apart as possible. They were widely used in 
early SER systems (Kaur & Singh, 2023). 
 — k-Nearest Neighbours (k-NN): k-NN classifies a new speech sample by checking which labelled 
samples it most closely resembles and assigning it the majority emotion among those neighbours 
(Kaur & Singh, 2023). 
 — Naïve Bayes: A simple probabilistic model that estimates which emotion is most likely based on the 
features, assuming each feature contributes independently (Kaur & Singh, 2023). 
 — Decision Trees / Random Forests: hierarchical partitioning; Decision trees split the data step by step 
based on feature values until they reach an emotion label. Random Forests combine many such trees, 
which makes them more stable and often more accurate, for example, outperforming SVMs on some 
SER datasets (Yan et al., 2020). 
 — Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs): GMMs represent each emotion as a combination of several 
Gaussian (bell-shaped) distributions. The model then estimates which emotion’s distribution best fits 
the input speech (Bishop, 2006).

 — Hidden Markov Models (HMMs): HMMs model speech as a sequence of short frames and capture how 
acoustic patterns change over time. They are especially useful for time-dependent signals like speech 
(Rabiner,1989). 
• Strengths and limitations: Conventional pipelines are computationally light, perform reasonably well with 
small, labelled datasets, and facilitate diagnostics (e.g., feature importance). However, performance 
strongly depends on the quality of the hand-crafted features, and classical models may face challenges 
when conditions change (e.g., speaker variation, noise, or language differences); limited multimodal fusion 
support is another constraint (Lian et al., 2023, Entropy).
6.4.2 Deep learning methods
• Modelling pipeline: Deep learning models tend to discover acoustic patterns on their own, whether they 
work directly with the waveform or with spectral representations. In doing so, they reduce the need for 
manually engineered features and instead discover informative representations automatically. A variety of 
neural encoder architectures are commonly used for this purpose. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) 
are effective for analysing the two-dimensional structure of spectrograms, capturing local spectro-temporal 
patterns. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), including LSTMs and GRUs, are suited to modelling how 
emotional cues evolve over time in the speech signal. Many SER systems combine these strengths 
through hybrid CNN–RNN models, which first extract local acoustic patterns and then learn their temporal 
dependencies. More recently, Transformer-based encoders have become prominent, using multi-head 
self-attention to capture long-range relationships across the speech sequence (Latif et al., 2023). 
• Representative deep learning model families:
 — Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): CNNs extract local patterns from spectrograms (e.g., pitch, 
formants, energy) and are very effective when SER is formulated as an image-like problem. They were 
among the first deep models to outperform classical MFCC+SVM pipelines (Neumann & Vu, 2017; Satt 
et al., 2017).
 — Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs): RNNs, especially LSTMs and GRUs, model the temporal dynamics 
of speech, capturing how emotions evolve across frames. They became a standard baseline for 
sequence modelling in SER before Transformers gained traction (Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Satt et al., 
2017).
 — CNN–RNN hybrids: Hybrid models combine CNNs for spectral feature extraction with RNNs for 
temporal modelling. This architecture is common in SER because it combines the strengths of both 
approaches: they capture local spectrotemporal details while also modelling how the signal evolves 
over time (Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Abdelhamid et al., 2022).
 — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs): learn compressed emotional representations without labels. They are 
used for feature learning, noise reduction, or generating synthetic emotional speech (Latif et al., 2018).

• Novelties:
 — Pretrained models: One of the biggest recent advances is the use of models like wav2vec 2.0 and

recognition. This helps a lot when emotional datasets are small and currently give some of the strongest 
results, especially for valence (Pepino et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2023).
 — Multimodal models: Deep learning also makes it easy to combine multiple signals at once, for example, 
speech together with facial expressions or text. Different “fusion” strategies (early, late or intermediate) 
are used to mix these modalities, and recent surveys summarise the main techniques and datasets in 
multimodal emotion recognition (Lian et al., 2023).
 — Data augmentation: Since emotional datasets are often small, data augmentation is increasingly used 
to improve model robustness. Typical techniques include pitch shifting, time-stretching, adding noise, 
SpecAugment, vocal tract length perturbation and synthetic data generation. These methods improve 
generalisation, especially for deep models working in low-resource conditions (Ko et al., 2015; Park et al., 
2019; Atmaja & Sasou, 2022; Chatziagapi et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2022).
• Strengths and limitations. Deep learning eliminates manual feature design, learns non ‑linear hierarchical 
patterns, scales with data, and integrates multimodal cues. However, these advantages come with 
trade‑offs: deep models usually require large amounts of labelled data (although this can be reduced through 
self‑supervised or transfer learning), they are harder to interpret, and they demand more computational 
resources during training and deployment (Latif et al., 2023; Wagner et al., 2023).

6.4.3 Is there an optimal model?
A recurrent theme in the literature is that there is no single optimal model for Speech Emotion Recognition (SER). As 
highlighted by De Lope and Graña (2023), SER encompasses a wide spectrum of classical machine learning methods 
and deep learning architectures, each with different strengths depending on the characteristics of the data and the task 
at hand. Their review shows that performance varies substantially across datasets, languages, emotional taxonomies, 
and feature extraction strategies, and that both classical and deep learning approaches continue to coexist in SER 
research. This diversity of methods reflects that model choice is inherently problemdependent rather than universal.
In practical terms, this means that the “best” model depends on what the researcher seeks to achieve, for 
example, maximising accuracy, ensuring interpretability, working with limited training data, or integrating multimodal 
inputs. As De Lope and Graña (2023) emphasise, SER systems are highly sensitive to dataset properties and 
experimental conditions, and no approach consistently outperforms all others across benchmarks. Thus, the field 
does not converge toward a single optimal classifier, but rather toward a set of techniques that must be matched to 
the specific requirements of each application.

7 Complementary Approach to SER
A complementary approach to Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is Natural Language Processing (NLP), which 
focuses on analysing the verbal content of speech rather than its acoustic properties. NLP requires converting 
the audio signal into text using an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system. Modern ASR pipelines, covered 
extensively in standard NLP textbooks, transform the speech waveform into linguistic units that can be processed 
computationally (Jurafsky & Martin, 2026). 
Once the speech is transcribed, NLP techniques can be applied to perform lexical, syntactic, and semantic 
analyses of the text. One widely used NLP application is Sentiment Analysis, which identifies explicit or implicit 
emotional content expressed through words, considering both word frequency and contextual meaning. Sentiment 
analysis is recognised as a core task within NLP , enabling the detection of attitudes, affect, and evaluative language 
in written or transcribed text (Ramdani, 2025; Jurafsky & Martin, 2026).

8.4 Create a model from scratch
Developing a custom SER system involves manually designing and integrating each component of the pipeline. This 
approach offers full control over how audio is processed, which features are extracted, and how the classifier is

• The workflow typically follows the previously reviewed five stages:
1. Audio acquisition: The process begins with selecting an audio source, either from existing emotional 
speech datasets such as EmoDB (Burkhardt et al., 2005), RAVDESS (Livingstone and Russo, 2018), or 
IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), or from self ‑recorded material.
2. Preprocessing: Before analysis, the audio must be cleaned and normalized to ensure consistent signal 
quality. Standard preprocessing steps include noise reduction, segmentation, silence trimming, and 
amplitude or sampling ‑rate normalization (De Lope & Graña, 2023; Katti & Sumana, 2023). These 
operations are essential because inadequate preprocessing negatively affects feature extraction and 
classifier performance.
3. Feature extraction: Once the signal is prepared, relevant acoustic properties are extracted. Emotional 
information is typically encoded in temporal, prosodic, spectral, and cepstral features, such as pitch, 
duration, energy, MFCCs, and formants—commonly used in traditional SER systems (De Lope & Graña, 
2023; Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023; Byun & Lee, 2021).
4. Classifier design: After feature extraction, a classifier is trained to map the acoustic descriptors to 
emotional categories. Conventional machine ‑learning methods include SVMs, k ‑NN, and Random 
Forests (Kaur & Singh, 2023; Yan et al., 2020), whereas deep‑learning approaches such as CNNs, RNNs, 
and hybrid CNN‑RNN architectures have become increasingly common for modelling both spectral and 
temporal patterns (Latif et al., 2023; Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Pepino et al., 2021).
5. Emotion prediction: Finally, the system outputs emotion labels or dimensional affect scores based on 
the trained model.

9 Discussion
9.1 Overview and Interpretation of the Synthesis
This review integrates evidence from psychophysiology, vocal acoustics, and contemporary Speech Emotion 
Recognition (SER) to clarify how emotional information is encoded and decoded through the human voice. Vocal 
expression arises from coordinated respiratory, laryngeal, and articulatory mechanisms that systematically shape 
acoustic features such as pitch, intensity, spectral balance, and temporal dynamics. From this perspective, SER is 
not only a classification task, but a modelling process grounded in how the vocal system functions physiologically 
and how these mechanisms give rise to measurable acoustic markers of affect.
9.2 Interdisciplinary Integration and Added Value
A major contribution of this review is the integration of domains that are often treated separately. By linking 
physiological mechanisms with acoustic correlates, psychological interpretation, and machinelearning 
methodologies, the review shows how internal states are translated into features that SER systems can 
analyse. This interdisciplinary perspective improves interpretability, supports more informed feature selection, 
and provides a stronger foundation for applications in HCI, HRI, and IoT, where systems must adapt to users’ 
emotional states.
9.3 Methodological Heterogeneity in SER
The field exhibits substantial heterogeneity at multiple levels:
• Data: emotional classifications, acted versus naturalistic speech, language coverage, recording 
conditions, and speaker diversity vary widely across databases; these factors directly affect benchmark 
comparability and model generalizability.
• Features and representations: The field ranges from using handcrafted features like prosody and MFCCs 
to relying on deep ‑learned and self ‑supervised representations, and this choice affects both model 
performance and the interpretability of the results.
• Modelling approaches: Classical machine ‑learning models still work well when data are limited and are 
easier to interpret, while deep learning, especially self ‑supervised models, delivers stronger performance 
and better transfer, but at the cost of more computation and lower interpretability. Given these sources of 
variation, there is no single optimal model for SER. Instead, model choice should be matched to the task, 
data regime, constraints on interpretability, and deployment context. 
9.4 Implications for Research and Practice
Connecting computational methods to what we know about how the voice works offers two clear benefits: 
First, it helps researchers make better decisions when choosing acoustic features and analysing errors. 
If a model misclassifies an emotion, the mistake can often be linked to specific physiological or articulatory 
factors—such as changes in vocalfold vibration or airflow—rather than being treated as an unexplained blackbox 
outcome.

In applied fields such as HCI, HRI, and IoT, this approach leads to systems that react more

Situated within the Neurocash ® methodology, SER can act as an additional, noninvasive bio-signal to complement 
gaze, tactility and other physiological measures when evaluating cash prototypes, both in laboratory and virtual 
neurodesign settings. By capturing vocal features associated with arousal, valence and cognitive load during 
taskoriented interactions with cash stimuli, SER could help predict acceptance, clarity and perceived security of 
design elements. Moreover, integrating SER with current Neurocash ® multimodal studies, such as EEG, gesture 
analysis and other biometric indicators, would provide a more holistic and robust view of implicit perception, 
enriching the project’s ability to identify how users emotionally and cognitively experience cashrelated designs.
9.6 Limitations of the Present Review
This work is a narrative integrative review rather than a systematic review or meta ‑analysis. As such, the goal 
was conceptual synthesis across heterogeneous literatures rather than quantitative aggregation. Because the 
sources span more than four decades of research (approximately 1980–2026), methodological conventions and 
technological capabilities vary considerably, which may limit direct comparability across studies. Although the 
search spanned multiple scholarly databases, preprint servers, and technical documentation, coverage cannot 
be exhaustive. In addition, the rapid pace of advances in deep learning and self ‑supervised speech modelling 
implies that specific tools and benchmarks may evolve quickly. Finally, while this review emphasizes physiological 
grounding and interdisciplinary integration, it does not resolve ongoing challenges in cross ‑lingual generalization, 
naturalistic emotion capture, and fine‑grained affect modelling (e.g., mixed emotions, appraisal dimensions, context 
dependence).
9.7 Future Directions
Building on the perspective developed in this review, several areas deserve attention:
• More natural and cross‑language data.
• Create larger and more diverse emotion‑speech datasets that:

10 Conclusion
This review has brought together different research domains to show that the human voice carries meaningful traces 
of emotional and cognitive activity. Rather than treating speech as a purely linguistic signal, the evidence reviewed 
here highlights how changes in respiration, vocal‑fold behaviour, and articulation leave measurable acoustic marks. 
These patterns —shifts in pitch, loudness, spectral balance, and timing — are not random; they reflect underlying 
psychophysiological states in ways that both psychologists and engineers can make use of.
Throughout the review, it has been emphasized that effective Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) depends 
as much on understanding how the voice works as on choosing the right computational tools. Clean preprocessing, 
thoughtful feature design or representation learning, and careful modelling choices are all important, but they make 
the most sense when grounded in vocal physiology and established acoustic correlations of emotion. Classical 
machine‑learning models are still relevant, especially when transparency or limited data are concerned, whereas 
deep and self ‑supervised approaches have opened the door to stronger generalization. Even so, the field has not 
identified a single optimal modelling “answer”, as it is unlikely that one model will satisfy all research needs.
For applications in Human Computer Interaction (HCI), Human Robot Interaction (HRI), Internet of Things 
(IoT), and related domains, including emerging frameworks such as Neurocash ®, SER can serve as an additional 
layer of information about users’ implicit reactions. Combining vocal cues via SER with NLP or with other biometric 
modalities seems promising, particularly when the goal is to capture subtle affective or cognitive shifts rather 
than explicit emotional displays. The success of these approaches, however, will likely depend on more diverse 
and naturalistic datasets, as well as clearer evaluation practices that consider label uncertainty and the mismatch 
between controlled laboratory data and real‑world settings. This becomes especially critical as perception studies for 
cash design have become increasingly important in recent years, demanding that the data obtained are sufficiently 
relevant to support reliable conclusions. In this context, modifying certain procedures—such as replacing on-screen 
response formats with the recording of participants’ vocal responses to questions presented on a screen—allows 
the direct application of SER to extract emotional information from speech, yielding richer data for cash design 
within the Neurocash® methodology.
Finally, advances in SER must be accompanied by responsible treatment of privacy, consent, and fairness. 
Voice is a personal biometric, and emotion inference can raise concerns beyond those encountered in traditional 
speech processing. Clear documentation, careful dataset construction, and transparent model reporting will be 
essential if voice ‑based affective technologies are to be used in a way that is both scientifically grounded and 
socially acceptable.

Abstract Situated within the Neurocash ® framework for measuring implicit emotional and cognitive responses, this review examines the human voice as a non-invasive psychophysiological marker. It outlines the physiological mechanisms of voice production and explains how emotional states influence breathing, vocal-fold vibration and articulation, shaping acoustic features such as pitch and intensity. The review then examines Speech Emotion Recognition as the main approach for extracting emotional information from speech, describing the methodological pipeline from emotional speech databases and preprocessing to classification using traditional machine-learning algorithms and modern deep-learning and self-supervised models. The analysis concludes that no single computational approach is universally optimal, as performance depends on language, emotional categories, data quality and environmental conditions. Overall, this review provides an interdisciplinary framework linking psychophysiology, vocal acoustics and artificial intelligence to support Neurocash® studies on cognitive workload, perceived security and implicit trust in cash design. Keywords: acoustic feature extraction, affective computing, implicit emotion perception, multimodal emotion analysis, psychophysiology, self-supervised representation learning, Speech Emotion Recognition, Neurocash®, cash design. JEL classification: C55, C80, D91.

Resumen A partir de la metodología Neurocash ® para el estudio de las respuestas emocionales y cognitivas implícitas, en este documento se examina la voz humana como un marcador psicofisiológico no invasivo. En primer lugar, se describen los mecanismos fisiológicos de producción de la voz y se explica cómo los estados emocionales modifican la respiración, la vibración de las cuerdas vocales y la articulación, lo que altera características acústicas como el tono y la intensidad. A continuación, se analiza el sistema de reconocimiento de emociones en el habla (SER, por sus siglas en inglés) como la principal herramienta para extraer información emocional a partir de la voz, describiendo su proceso metodológico desde la selección de bases de datos y el preprocesamiento hasta la clasificación mediante algoritmos de aprendizaje automático clásico y modelos de aprendizaje profundo y autosupervisado. El análisis concluye que no existe un modelo universalmente óptimo y proporciona un marco interdisciplinar para apoyar estudios Neurocash® sobre carga cognitiva, seguridad percibida y confianza implícita en el diseño del efectivo. BANCO DE ESPAÑA 9 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 1 Introduction Cash design is not only a matter of visual aesthetics and security features, but also of how people implicitly perceive, interpret, and emotionally respond to cash during daily interactions. In this context, voice analysis offers a promising bridge between cash perception research and psychophysiological measurement, as vocal signals can reflect subtle changes in emotional arousal, cognitive load, confidence, and perceived security. Understanding these implicit human reactions is fundamental in cash design to optimize currency usability and the effectiveness of anti-counterfeiting measures. The aim of this review is to offer a broad and connected perspective on voice analysis, encompassing the physiological bases of vocal production, its relationship with emotional expression, and the technological tools currently available for extracting acoustic features in perception and affective-computing research. In doing so, the work synthesizes the present state of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) technologies while preserving a conceptual and accessible perspective grounded in psychology. Rather than offering an exhaustive technical review of every computational component, the goal is to present a coherent, interdisciplinary overview that bridges psychophysiology, acoustics, and machine-learning approaches to emotional voice analysis. SER is situated within the broader domain of Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER), a field that integrates multiple biosignals, such as EEG (electroencephalography), facial expressions, gestures, or speech, to infer affective states. Within this ecosystem, the human voice stands out as a unique psychophysiological signal: it arises from the coordination of breathing, vocal-fold movement, and articulation, all of which change with emotional, cognitive, and autonomic states (De Lope & Graña, 2023). Understanding these biological mechanisms is therefore essential for interpreting how emotions shape the acoustic signal. For this reason, the document begins by outlining the physiological and anatomical bases of vocal production, following authors who argue that acoustic analyses must be

grounded in vocal biomechanics. Building on this theoretical foundation, the second section examines how emotional states influence key acoustic features such as fundamental frequency, intensity, spectral balance, and temporal dynamics. Recent reviews show that emotions reliably shape vocal acoustics, allowing speech to convey meaningful psychophysiological information (Van Puyvelde et al., 2018; Schewski et al., 2025). These relationships are central both to psychological research and to the development of computational models that aim to decode emotions from speech. The study then presents the complete Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) methodological pipeline, outlining the process of transforming raw audio into emotional labels. These stages include audio-source selection, preprocessing, acoustic feature extraction, and classification using either classical machine-learning algorithms or modern deep-learning architectures. Finally, after describing the pipeline, the document provides a structured overview of the most relevant technological tools for implementing SER, ranging from commercial to open-source options. This includes commercial approaches (e.g., audEERING, iMotions), pretrained model pipelines with external or internal classifiers, custom SER systems built from scratch, and modular multimodal frameworks such as the MixedEmotions Toolbox. By comparing these alternatives, practical considerations that researchers must evaluate when selecting tools for academic or applied contexts are highlighted, including model interpretability, data requirements, and computational costs.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 10 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 Although this review focuses on the human voice as a neurophysiological marker for implicit emotion, it is motivated by the broader research context of neurodesign for cash. Within the Neurocash ® framework, the Innovation & Development unit of the Banco de España aims to establish an objective, multidimensional methodology to evaluate the public’s perception of banknotes. By integrating neuroscientific tools and implicit behavioral measures, this project seeks to overcome the traditional limitations of subjective surveys, capturing the subconscious emotional and cognitive reactions of users when interacting with currency (Banco de España, n.d.; Ortuño et al., 2020). Specifically applied to cash perception research, the Neurocash ® methodology provides cash designers with a robust, quantitative tool to optimize the design process. By capturing these acoustic fluctuations during exposure to or evaluation of currency features, the human voice can complement other biometric and behavioral measures within this framework. This allows for the precise evaluation of how different visual and tactile elements capture attention, how cognitive workload is modulated during the verification of security features, and how these factors influence the user’s implicit trust and perceived security (Banco de España, n.d.; Ortuño et al., 2020). By systematically analyzing these biometric, neurophysiological, and vocal responses, Neurocash ® acts as a scientific bridge that enhances the aesthetics, intuitive usability, and anti-counterfeiting resilience of banknotes throughout their entire lifecycle. 1.1 Justification of the review Despite the rapid growth of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), existing reviews remain fragmented and often focus on only one part of the field. Most surveys highlight technical advances, especially, new machine-learning models and self-supervised speech methods, while giving much less attention to the psychophysiological and acoustic principles that support emotional expression in the voice. As a result, many overviews adopt a mainly computational viewpoint, with

limited connection to the biological mechanisms of vocal production or to the well-established acoustic markers of emotion. This limitation in the review literature reflects a broader problem in the field: a lack of integration across disciplines. Psychophysiology, vocal acoustics, and deep-learning-based SER systems are often treated as separate research areas, even though they naturally depend on one another. Because of this separation, key concepts, such as subglottal pressure changes, vocal-fold behaviour, prosodic shifts, and spectral patterns, rarely appear together in computational surveys. This reduces the interpretability of SER models and makes it harder to understand the psychophysiological meaning of the features these systems extract. A further challenge is that research on how emotions influence vocal acoustics is spread across different fields such as clinical voice science, neuroscience, phonetics, and machine learning. Because these findings are rarely brought together, it is difficult to build a clear, unified understanding of how emotional processes shape the voice and how these cues are used in SER systems. For these reasons, an integrative review that unifies physiological mechanisms, acoustic correlates, psychological theory, and contemporary SER methodologies is necessary. The present work aims to consolidate these domains into a coherent conceptual framework, offering the scientific community a comprehensive, interdisciplinary account of how emotions are encoded and decoded through the human voice.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 11 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 2 Methods This article was written as a narrative integrative review, a method that brings together different types of evidence from fields such as psychophysiology, acoustics, speech science, affective computing, and machine learning. This type of review makes it possible to combine empirical studies, theoretical work, technical documentation, and methodological papers to create a broad understanding of a research area. Because Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) involves many disciplines, this approach is well suited to summarizing its physiological, acoustic, and computational aspects within a single framework. 2.1 Search Strategy and Sources Between October 2025 and February 2026, a broad literature search was performed across the following databases and platforms: • Google Scholar • PubMed (physiology, voice science) • IEEE Xplore (machine learning, signal processing) • ACM Digital Library [Human Computer Interaction (HCI), affective computing] • arXiv (deep learning and transformer-based SER studies) • Publisher websites for technical documentation (e.g., audEERING, iMotions, Affectiva, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services) • GitHub repositories for open-source SER toolkits. The search combined keywords and Boolean operators such as: “speech emotion recognition” OR “SER” OR “emotional prosody” OR “acoustic correlates of emotion” OR “self-supervised speech models” OR “wav2vec2” OR “HuBERT” OR “WavLM” OR “affective computing” OR “voice physiology” OR “emotion acoustics”. 2.2 Inclusion Criteria Sources were included if they met at least one of the following criteria: • Conceptual relevance to the physiological, psychological, or computational foundations of emotional voice production (e.g., Liebenthal et al., 2016). • Empirical or methodological contribution to acoustic correlates of emotion, vocal stress, or prosody (e.g., Van Puyvelde et al., 2018; Schewski et al., 2025).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 12 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 • Technical relevance to SER pipelines, preprocessing, feature sets, or databases (e.g., openSMILE, GeMAPS, EmoDB, RAVDESS, IEMOCAP). • Machine learning or deep learning significance (e.g., de Lope & Graña, 2023; Kaur & Singh, 2023; Latif et al., 2023; Baevski et al., 2020; Hsu et al., 2021). • Applied frameworks in HCI, IoT, or affective technologies (e.g., Chang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). • Commercial and tool documentation, when necessary to describe real world SER implementations (e.g., audEERING, iMotions, Affectiva). 2.3 Exclusion Criteria • Studies unrelated to emotional voice analysis or without a clear methodological contribution. • Papers focused exclusively on Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) without relevance to emotion or prosody. • Non scholarly sources lacking technical or conceptual value. • Duplicated versions of the same paper (e.g., arXiv version and published journal version; only one was retained). 2.4 Selection and Synthesis Process Rather than filtering the literature in a strict, linear way, the review built its themes gradually through several cycles of reading and analysis. 1. Initial screening of titles and abstracts to identify relevance. 2. Full-text assessment of a large corpus of documents (approx. 80–100) dated between 1980–2026 3. Thematic clustering into core domains: — Vocal physiology and how the voice is produced (breathing, vocal folds, and articulation). — How emotions shape the acoustic signal (changes in pitch/F0, loudness, voice quality, and timing). — The SER pipeline (audio collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, and classification methods). — Emotional speech datasets used for training and evaluation (e.g., EmoDB, RAVDESS, IEMOCAP). — Types of acoustic features (prosodic, spectral, cepstral, energy related, temporal/fluency features, and standard sets like eGeMAPS).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 13 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 — Modelling approaches in SER (classical machine learning, deep learning models, and self supervised/ pretrained speech models). — Implementation options and tools (commercial platforms, pretrained models with or without external classifiers, full custom pipelines, and multimodal frameworks like MixedEmotions). — Complementary NLP methods (ASR to text combined with sentiment or affect analysis). 4. Cross disciplinary integration, linking psychophysiology with computational modelling to construct a coherent conceptual narrative. Because integrative reviews focus on conceptual synthesis rather than performing statistical analyses, no formal quality-assessment tools (such as PRISMA or GRADE) were used. Instead, priority was given to selecting recent, rigorous, influential sources that showed consistency with findings from other studies.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 14 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 3 Definition and Applications of SER 3.1 Definition Within the broader field of Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER), which includes analyses based on EEG, gestures, facial expressions, and other biometric signals, we find Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), whose primary function is to convert audio into text. This process relies on signal processing and machine learning methods that are shared with emotion related systems (De Lope & Graña, 2023). One of ASR’s key subfields is Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), which uses similar signal processing tools such as speech rate, pitch, and prosody to identify and classify emotions present in speech. Recent work highlights the importance of these acoustic cues in predicting emotional states accurately (Van Puyvelde et al., 2018; Schewski et al., 2025). 3.2 Applications SER is used in many areas, including psychology, healthcare, and marketing. However, for the purposes of this work, in the context of implicit perception measurement, we focus on its role within the Internet of Things (IoT). In IoT environments, devices interact continuously with users, and emotional information can help these systems adjust their behaviour, personalise their responses, and create more natural interactions (Chang et al., 2024). The IoT ecosystem includes several interaction focused fields, such as Human–Computer Interaction (HCI), Human– Machine Interaction (HMI), Human–Robot Interaction (HRI), and Affective Computing. Within this ecosystem, SER becomes especially relevant for Affective Computing, a field whose goal is to detect and interpret human emotions so that systems can adapt affectively. This “affective layer” is what distinguishes Affective Computing from other interaction oriented disciplines: • HCI, HMI, and HRI focus on the mechanics and design of interaction, such as interfaces, usability, ergonomics, and task performance, without necessarily analysing emotional states. • Affective Computing, in contrast, explicitly incorporates emotion. It studies how machines can understand
and respond to the user’s affective signals (Wang et al., 2022), making SER a key component for enabling emotionally adaptive behaviour.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 15 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 4 Voice Physiology and Acoustic Correlates of Emotion As illustrated in Figure 1, voice production begins with airflow originating in the lungs. The vocal folds, two bands of tissue located in the larynx between the base of the tongue and the top of the trachea, remain open during breathing and close during phonation (National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders [NIDCD, n.d.]). When speaking, the diaphragm contracts to expand the thoracic cavity, allowing the lungs to fill with air before releasing it during exhalation, which initiates the phonatory process (Ladefoged, 2001). Sound is produced when exhaled air passes through the closed vocal folds, increasing subglottal pressure until they separate, allowing air to flow through the glottis. The glottis widens during breathing and narrows during voice production (NIDCD, n.d.; Zhang, 2016). Rapid airflow creates pressure changes that bring the vocal folds back together, causing them to vibrate and generate sound. Typical speech requires normal vibratory behaviour of both the larynx and the vocal folds (Morrison, Rammage, Nichol, Pullan, & May, 1994). Once phonation is understood, further components of speech production can be defined, namely articulation and resonance. BANCO DE ESPAÑA 17 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 5 Emotions and their Influence on Acoustics Emotions influence the way our voice sounds because they affect how we breathe, how the larynx is positioned, and how the vocal tract moves. In psychology, emotions are understood as complex reactions that include thoughts, bodily changes, and expressive behaviours, all of which can shape our vocal output (American Psychological Association [APA], n.d.). Research shows that emotional states modify key acoustic features, such as fundamental frequency (F0), loudness, spectral balance or voice quality, and timing, through physiological changes in subglottal pressure, vocal fold vibration, and the configuration of the vocal tract (Liebenthal et al., 2016; Van Puyvelde et al., 2018). For example, positive emotions often occur alongside facial and postural changes like smiling, which alter the shape of the vocal tract and tend to produce a higher, brighter ‑sounding voice. More generally, high ‑arousal emotions such as joy or anger are associated with louder voices and greater variation in intensity than low ‑arousal states like sadness or tenderness (Liebenthal et al., 2016). Emotional and cognitive demands also influence vocal behaviour. When people are under cognitive– emotional load, their voices show measurable shifts in F0, loudness, and perturbation ‑based voice measures, reflecting the combined effect of attention, mental effort, and affective state on vocal production (Van Mersbergen & Payne, 2021; Van Puyvelde et al., 2018). Clinical reviews further show that increased tension in the larynx can produce rougher voice quality and reduced vocal power, illustrating how physiological stress and emotional strain affect the sound of the voice (Eastwood et al., 2015). Taken together, these findings support the idea that emotions influence speech through coordinated changes in bodily, cognitive, and expressive systems, consistent with the three‑component model of emotion. A growing body of research demonstrates that emotions

also shape prosody, patterns of pitch, rhythm, and intonation, in reliable ways. A large review of speech produced under negative emotions, stress, and cognitive load shows that anger, fear, anxiety, and stress frequently involve increases in F0 and, in some cases, noticeable changes in speech rate or pausing, although results vary across studies (Schewski et al., 2025). Evidence from acted emotional speech in Mexican Spanish similarly reveals distinct prosodic profiles: emocionado [excited] and enojado [angry] show high F0 values, wide pitch movements, and rising bitonal accents, while tranquilo [calm] and triste [sad] display flatter, more even pitch contours with smaller differences between syllables. Neutral utterances follow the expected declarative pattern typical of Central Mexican Spanish (González Franco et al., 2023).

Recent reviews group these properties into several main categories, temporal, prosodic, spectral, cepstral, and energy‑related features, and describe standardized feature sets developed for paralinguistic analysis (De Lope & Graña, 2023; Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023). 6.3.1 Temporal and fluency features Temporal features describe how speech unfolds over time. They include overall duration, speech rate, syllable timing, rhythm, and the presence or length of pauses, as well as distinctions between vocalic and non ‑vocalic segments. These patterns often change with emotional arousal or cognitive load and are frequently included in both traditional feature sets and deep‑learning SER models (Byun & Lee, 2021; De Lope & Graña, 2023). 6.3.2 Prosodic features Prosodic features relate to pitch and loudness patterns, such as fundamental frequency (F0), intonation contours, intensity, accentuation, and overall variability. Because they reflect adjustments in phonation and respiration, prosodic cues are reliably associated with emotional expression in speech (Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023; De Lope & Graña, 2023). 6.3.3 Spectral features Spectral features capture how energy is distributed across frequencies. They include formants, spectral centroid, roll‑off, kurtosis, and various energy bands, as well as spectrogram‑based representations such as Mel‑spectrograms. These features reflect vocal ‑tract configuration and are essential in both classical machine ‑learning and deep learning–based SER systems (Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023). 6.3.4 Cepstral features Widely used in speech and emotion recognition, cepstral coefficients such as MFCCs, delta and delta

‑delta coefficients, GFCCs, and LPCCs capture perceptually and physiologically meaningful aspects of the signal. Many SER studies adopt them as core inputs for both machine ‑learning and neural architectures (Byun & Lee, 2021; Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023). 6.3.5 Energy‑based features Energy features measure the overall power of the signal and its variation over time. Metrics such as root mean square (RMS) energy can help differentiate high ‑arousal from low‑arousal emotional states (Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 22 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 6.4 Classifier Approaches: Conventional (Classical Machine Learning) vs. Deep Learning Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems are commonly divided into two major methodological families. The first relies on conventional machine ‑learning models built on hand ‑crafted acoustic features, while the second uses deep learning techniques that learn informative representations directly from the speech signal or from its time–frequency transformations. This section provides an overview of the modelling assumptions, typical input features, representative algorithms, and the main advantages and limitations associated with each approach. A comprehensive survey of the field discusses these developments in detail and motivates the comparison presented here (Kaur & Singh, 2023). 6.4.1 Conventional methods (classical machine learning) • Modelling pipeline: Conventional Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) methods begin by extracting a set of hand-crafted features from the audio signal. These features describe core aspects of the voice, such as pitch, loudness, rhythmic patterns, and widely used acoustic descriptors like Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), which summarise how energy is distributed across frequency bands. After these features are obtained, they are passed to a traditional machine-learning classifier, such as Support Vector Machines, k-Nearest Neighbours, Naïve Bayes, decision trees or Random Forests, Gaussian Mixture Models, or Hidden Markov Models, which learns to distinguish between emotional categories. Because these features are manually designed rather than learned automatically, this approach tends to work reliably even when only limited training data are available. It is also generally considered more transparent and easier to interpret than modern deep-learning systems. MFCCs, in particular, have a long history in speech processing research, originating in the influential work of Davis and Mermelstein (1980). • Representative classifiers: — Support Vector Machines (SVMs): SVMs try to find the best boundary that separates different emotion classes in the feature space, keeping the classes as

far apart as possible. They were widely used in early SER systems (Kaur & Singh, 2023). — k-Nearest Neighbours (k-NN): k-NN classifies a new speech sample by checking which labelled samples it most closely resembles and assigning it the majority emotion among those neighbours (Kaur & Singh, 2023). — Naïve Bayes: A simple probabilistic model that estimates which emotion is most likely based on the features, assuming each feature contributes independently (Kaur & Singh, 2023). — Decision Trees / Random Forests: hierarchical partitioning; Decision trees split the data step by step based on feature values until they reach an emotion label. Random Forests combine many such trees, which makes them more stable and often more accurate, for example, outperforming SVMs on some SER datasets (Yan et al., 2020). — Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs): GMMs represent each emotion as a combination of several Gaussian (bell-shaped) distributions. The model then estimates which emotion’s distribution best fits the input speech (Bishop, 2006).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 23 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 — Hidden Markov Models (HMMs): HMMs model speech as a sequence of short frames and capture how acoustic patterns change over time. They are especially useful for time-dependent signals like speech (Rabiner,1989). • Strengths and limitations: Conventional pipelines are computationally light, perform reasonably well with small, labelled datasets, and facilitate diagnostics (e.g., feature importance). However, performance strongly depends on the quality of the hand-crafted features, and classical models may face challenges when conditions change (e.g., speaker variation, noise, or language differences); limited multimodal fusion support is another constraint (Lian et al., 2023, Entropy). 6.4.2 Deep learning methods • Modelling pipeline: Deep learning models tend to discover acoustic patterns on their own, whether they work directly with the waveform or with spectral representations. In doing so, they reduce the need for manually engineered features and instead discover informative representations automatically. A variety of neural encoder architectures are commonly used for this purpose. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are effective for analysing the two-dimensional structure of spectrograms, capturing local spectro-temporal patterns. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), including LSTMs and GRUs, are suited to modelling how emotional cues evolve over time in the speech signal. Many SER systems combine these strengths through hybrid CNN–RNN models, which first extract local acoustic patterns and then learn their temporal dependencies. More recently, Transformer-based encoders have become prominent, using multi-head self-attention to capture long-range relationships across the speech sequence (Latif et al., 2023). • Representative deep learning model families: — Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): CNNs extract local patterns from spectrograms (e.g., pitch, formants, energy) and are very effective when SER is formulated as an image-like problem. They were among the first deep models to outperform classical MFCC+SVM pipelines (Neumann & Vu, 2017; Satt et al., 2017). — Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs):

RNNs, especially LSTMs and GRUs, model the temporal dynamics of speech, capturing how emotions evolve across frames. They became a standard baseline for sequence modelling in SER before Transformers gained traction (Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Satt et al., 2017). — CNN–RNN hybrids: Hybrid models combine CNNs for spectral feature extraction with RNNs for temporal modelling. This architecture is common in SER because it combines the strengths of both approaches: they capture local spectrotemporal details while also modelling how the signal evolves over time (Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Abdelhamid et al., 2022). — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs): learn compressed emotional representations without labels. They are used for feature learning, noise reduction, or generating synthetic emotional speech (Latif et al., 2018).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 24 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 — Transformer-based models: Transformers use self-attention to model long-range dependencies and have become the most powerful architecture in SER. Pretrained variants like wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT dominate current benchmarks (Pepino et al., 2021; Latif et al., 2023). — Supervised vs. Self-supervised learning: • Supervised learning requires labelled emotional audio and was the traditional setup for CNN/RNN models. Its performance depends strongly on dataset size and annotation quality (Trigeorgis et al., 2016). • Self-supervised learning (SSL) learns general speech features from unlabelled audio (e.g., wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT), achieving far better generalisation in low-resource emotional datasets (Hsu et al., 2021; Pepino et al., 2021). • Novelties: — Pretrained models: One of the biggest recent advances is the use of models like wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT. They are first trained on huge amounts of unlabelled audio and then fine-tuned for emotion recognition. This helps a lot when emotional datasets are small and currently give some of the strongest results, especially for valence (Pepino et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2023). — Multimodal models: Deep learning also makes it easy to combine multiple signals at once, for example, speech together with facial expressions or text. Different “fusion” strategies (early, late or intermediate) are used to mix these modalities, and recent surveys summarise the main techniques and datasets in multimodal emotion recognition (Lian et al., 2023). — Data augmentation: Since emotional datasets are often small, data augmentation is increasingly used to improve model robustness. Typical techniques include pitch shifting, time-stretching, adding noise, SpecAugment, vocal tract length perturbation and synthetic data generation. These methods improve generalisation, especially for deep models working in low-resource conditions (Ko et al., 2015; Park et al., 2019; Atmaja & Sasou, 2022; Chatziagapi et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2022).

• Strengths and limitations. Deep learning eliminates manual feature design, learns non ‑linear hierarchical patterns, scales with data, and integrates multimodal cues. However, these advantages come with trade‑offs: deep models usually require large amounts of labelled data (although this can be reduced through self‑supervised or transfer learning), they are harder to interpret, and they demand more computational resources during training and deployment (Latif et al., 2023; Wagner et al., 2023). As highlighted by De Lope and Graña (2023), SER encompasses a wide spectrum of classical machine learning methods and deep learning architectures, each with different strengths depending on the characteristics of the data and the task at hand. In practical terms, this means that the “best” model depends on what the researcher seeks to achieve, for example, maximising accuracy, ensuring interpretability, working with limited training data, or integrating multimodal inputs. Audio acquisition: The process begins with selecting an audio source, either from existing emotional speech datasets such as EmoDB (Burkhardt et al., 2005), RAVDESS (Livingstone and Russo, 2018), or IEMOCAP (Busso et al., 2008), or from self ‑recorded material. 2. Preprocessing: Before analysis, the audio must be cleaned and normalized to ensure consistent signal quality. Standard preprocessing steps include noise reduction, segmentation, silence trimming, and amplitude or sampling ‑rate normalization (De Lope & Graña, 2023; Katti & Sumana, 2023). These operations are essential because inadequate preprocessing negatively affects feature extraction and classifier performance. 3. Feature extraction: Once the signal is prepared, relevant acoustic properties are extracted. Emotional information is typically encoded in temporal, prosodic, spectral, and cepstral features, such as pitch, duration, energy, MFCCs, and formants—commonly used in traditional SER systems (De Lope & Graña, 2023; Bhangale & Kothandaraman, 2023; Byun & Lee, 2021). 4. Classifier design: After feature extraction, a classifier is trained to map the acoustic descriptors to emotional categories. Conventional machine ‑learning methods include SVMs, k ‑NN, and Random Forests (Kaur & Singh, 2023; Yan et al., 2020), whereas deep‑learning approaches such as CNNs, RNNs, and hybrid CNN‑RNN architectures have become increasingly common for modelling both spectral and temporal patterns (Latif et al., 2023; Trigeorgis et al., 2016; Pepino et al., 2021). 5. Emotion prediction: Finally, the system outputs emotion labels or dimensional affect scores based on the trained model.
