The MixedEmotions Toolbox provides a unified framework that enables automatic extraction of emotions across modalities and supports lexical and semantic analysis. For Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), the toolbox includes the “Emotion Recognition Audio (m6)” module, which implements a complete SER pipeline—from acoustic feature extraction to modelbased emotion prediction—returning continuous affect estimates such as arousal and valence (Buitelaar et al., 2018). The platform can be downloaded from GitHub and executed using Docker containers, as each module is packaged as an independent microservice that can be deployed without dependency issues (Buitelaar et al., 2018).

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 32 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 9 Discussion 9.1 Overview and Interpretation of the Synthesis This review integrates evidence from psychophysiology, vocal acoustics, and contemporary Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) to clarify how emotional information is encoded and decoded through the human voice. Vocal expression arises from coordinated respiratory, laryngeal, and articulatory mechanisms that systematically shape acoustic features such as pitch, intensity, spectral balance, and temporal dynamics. From this perspective, SER is not only a classification task, but a modelling process grounded in how the vocal system functions physiologically and how these mechanisms give rise to measurable acoustic markers of affect. 9.2 Interdisciplinary Integration and Added Value A major contribution of this review is the integration of domains that are often treated separately. By linking physiological mechanisms with acoustic correlates, psychological interpretation, and machinelearning methodologies, the review shows how internal states are translated into features that SER systems can analyse. This interdisciplinary perspective improves interpretability, supports more informed feature selection, and provides a stronger foundation for applications in HCI, HRI, and IoT, where systems must adapt to users’ emotional states. 9.3 Methodological Heterogeneity in SER The field exhibits substantial heterogeneity at multiple levels: • Data: emotional classifications, acted versus naturalistic speech, language coverage, recording conditions, and speaker diversity vary widely across databases; these factors directly affect benchmark comparability and model generalizability. • Features and representations: The field ranges from using handcrafted features like prosody and MFCCs to relying on deep ‑learned and self ‑supervised representations, and this choice affects both model performance and the interpretability of the results. • Modelling approaches: Classical machine ‑learning models still work well when data are limited and are easier to interpret, while deep learning, especially self ‑supervised models, delivers stronger performance and better transfer, but at the cost of more computation and lower

interpretability. Given these sources of variation, there is no single optimal model for SER. Instead, model choice should be matched to the task, data regime, constraints on interpretability, and deployment context. 9.4 Implications for Research and Practice Connecting computational methods to what we know about how the voice works offers two clear benefits: First, it helps researchers make better decisions when choosing acoustic features and analysing errors. If a model misclassifies an emotion, the mistake can often be linked to specific physiological or articulatory factors—such as changes in vocalfold vibration or airflow—rather than being treated as an unexplained blackbox outcome.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 33 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 Second, incorporating knowledge about vocal behaviour into the model design allows developers to include constraints that reflect how real speech is produced. These constraints, whether introduced through architecture or the training process, make the system more robust when dealing with background noise, different speakers, or natural variation in emotional expression. In applied fields such as HCI, HRI, and IoT, this approach leads to systems that react more appropriately to users’ emotions while remaining interpretable for developers and practitioners. In studies related to cash perception, these methods can help analyse emotional and cognitive reactions to cash design and perceptions of security. This aligns with the goals of the Neurocash ® framework, which focuses on understanding emotional impact, cognitive processing, visual impact, and the public’s sense of safety when interacting with cash (Banco de España, n.d.; Ortuño et al., 2020). 9.5 Potential Application to Cash Perception Research Situated within the Neurocash ® methodology, SER can act as an additional, noninvasive bio-signal to complement gaze, tactility and other physiological measures when evaluating cash prototypes, both in laboratory and virtual neurodesign settings. By capturing vocal features associated with arousal, valence and cognitive load during taskoriented interactions with cash stimuli, SER could help predict acceptance, clarity and perceived security of design elements. Moreover, integrating SER with current Neurocash ® multimodal studies, such as EEG, gesture analysis and other biometric indicators, would provide a more holistic and robust view of implicit perception, enriching the project’s ability to identify how users emotionally and cognitively experience cashrelated designs. 9.6 Limitations of the Present Review This work is a narrative integrative review rather than a systematic review or meta ‑analysis. As such, the goal was conceptual synthesis across heterogeneous literatures rather than quantitative aggregation. Because the sources span more than four

decades of research (approximately 1980–2026), methodological conventions and technological capabilities vary considerably, which may limit direct comparability across studies. Although the search spanned multiple scholarly databases, preprint servers, and technical documentation, coverage cannot be exhaustive. In addition, the rapid pace of advances in deep learning and self ‑supervised speech modelling implies that specific tools and benchmarks may evolve quickly. Finally, while this review emphasizes physiological grounding and interdisciplinary integration, it does not resolve ongoing challenges in cross ‑lingual generalization, naturalistic emotion capture, and fine‑grained affect modelling (e.g., mixed emotions, appraisal dimensions, context dependence). 9.7 Future Directions Building on the perspective developed in this review, several areas deserve attention: • More natural and cross‑language data. • Create larger and more diverse emotion‑speech datasets that: — Use clear and consistent ways of labelling emotions.

This would help systems work better across different people, contexts, and languages. • Models guided by how the voice works physically: Design models that consider what we know about voice production, for example, how pitch changes, how air pressure works, or how the tongue and lips move when emotions shift. Combining these understandable features with modern deep ‑learning methods may make systems stronger and easier to interpret. • Understanding implicit emotion and multimodality: Develop studies and models that focus on implicit emotional signals, not only on explicit emotion labels. Additionally, evaluate multimodal systems that combine different sources of information, such as speech, text, facial expressions, and physiological signals, and systematically remove one source at a time to clearly identify the contribution of each modality. • Better evaluation and more transparency: Develop testing standards that consider: — Uncertainty in emotion labels. — Unbalanced datasets. — Changes between training and real‑world conditions. — Pair performance scores with tools that show what parts of the sound the system paid attention to, and whether those parts match known acoustic patterns. • Responsible and fair deployment: For real ‑world applications (HCI, HRI, IoT), make sure systems handle privacy, consent, and fairness properly. This means documenting how data were collected, who is represented in the dataset, and how the system was checked for bias, not just for technical accuracy.

BANCO DE ESPAÑA 35 DOCUMENTO OCASIONAL N.º 2618 10 Conclusion This review has brought together different research domains to show that the human voice carries meaningful traces of emotional and cognitive activity. Rather than treating speech as a purely linguistic signal, the evidence reviewed here highlights how changes in respiration, vocal‑fold behaviour, and articulation leave measurable acoustic marks. These patterns —shifts in pitch, loudness, spectral balance, and timing — are not random; they reflect underlying psychophysiological states in ways that both psychologists and engineers can make use of. Throughout the review, it has been emphasized that effective Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) depends as much on understanding how the voice works as on choosing the right computational tools. Clean preprocessing, thoughtful feature design or representation learning, and careful modelling choices are all important, but they make the most sense when grounded in vocal physiology and established acoustic correlations of emotion. Classical machine‑learning models are still relevant, especially when transparency or limited data are concerned, whereas deep and self ‑supervised approaches have opened the door to stronger generalization. Even so, the field has not identified a single optimal modelling “answer”, as it is unlikely that one model will satisfy all research needs. For applications in Human Computer Interaction (HCI), Human Robot Interaction (HRI), Internet of Things (IoT), and related domains, including emerging frameworks such as Neurocash ®, SER can serve as an additional layer of information about users’ implicit reactions. Combining vocal cues via SER with NLP or with other biometric modalities seems promising, particularly when the goal is to capture subtle affective or cognitive shifts rather than explicit emotional displays. The success of these approaches, however, will likely depend on more diverse and naturalistic datasets, as well as clearer evaluation practices that consider label uncertainty and the mismatch between controlled laboratory

data and real‑world settings. This becomes especially critical as perception studies for cash design have become increasingly important in recent years, demanding that the data obtained are sufficiently relevant to support reliable conclusions. In this context, modifying certain procedures—such as replacing on-screen response formats with the recording of participants’ vocal responses to questions presented on a screen—allows the direct application of SER to extract emotional information from speech, yielding richer data for cash design within the Neurocash® methodology. Finally, advances in SER must be accompanied by responsible treatment of privacy, consent, and fairness. Voice is a personal biometric, and emotion inference can raise concerns beyond those encountered in traditional speech processing. Clear documentation, careful dataset construction, and transparent model reporting will be essential if voice ‑based affective technologies are to be used in a way that is both scientifically grounded and socially acceptable.
